title: Act II, Prologue

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus reports that Romeo's old love has died and a new one replaced it; both lovers are bewitched by looks. As enemies they cannot meet freely, but passion gives them the power and time the means.

context.history: Choruses between acts were less common in English plays than in classical drama; this is the only one between acts in the play.

significance: It frames the next act and invites the audience to judge the speed of Romeo's change.
discussionQuestions: How fast can someone fall out of love and into a new one?
Where does structure appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with violence and the feud?

An argument about structure and audience guidance. The evidence is “Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir” (Act II, Prologue, Chorus) — Romeo's love for Rosaline dies; a new one takes its place. This develops love and desire: the Chorus questions how fast Romeo's love moved from Rosaline to Juliet. "Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir," and both lovers are "betwitched by the charm of looks.".

Earlier, in Act I, Scene V, Romeo, the text reads “O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright” — Juliet as light in darkness. Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie,
And young affection gapes to be his heir;
That fair for which love groan’d for and would die,
With tender Juliet match’d, is now not fair.

And she steal love’s sweet bait from fearful hooks:

To breathe such vows as lovers use to swear;

To meet her new-beloved any where:

Tempering extremities with extreme sweet. Exit.
